text: Two weeks of SSH shows regular command-only deploy logins from the monitoring host and key-based CI. No failed login is being treated as a breach. Removed unneeded root rsync, expired unlisted contractor jpark, blocked execution under writable upload/cache trees, removed root execution of WordPress from orders metrics.

CI release uses push, not agent forwarding. Maintenance uses only local root-owned steps; git garbage collection now drops to repo owner. Expired unlisted contractor, protected backup env and repo config, restricted database-transfer key to db-01 and pinned known web host key.

No anomalous database grants to the web app: wordpress only. Restricted plaintext dump staging and transient archive creation to root. Invoice corrections now require the submitted amount to match the referenced order; outstanding differences were not overwritten.

Restricted plugin support endpoints to authenticated admins and required a nonce for cache deletion. PHP worker can still write uploads/cache, not executable site code. Export helper now enforces marketing vs support roles, bounds ID lookups, stages privately and drops privilege before creating user output. Removed unnecessary recursive root ownership changes during releases.
Restricted archive receiver to write-only rsync in its archive directory; changed both senders to use that directory as transfer root. Tested a real encrypted dump and transfer.

Mia: 172.58.225.22 was absent pre-migration. 17:53 pts/0 exported then printed all 41 newsletter rows, unlike routine 5-row previews. At 17:57 pts/3 checked id and sudo -l while known home IP had pts/4 doing legitimate marketing. Rotated only her password. Suspect sessions closed before rotation; preserved the legitimate session and verified no new authorized key.

18:00:45 a previously unused old Air SSH key for the compromised account from a second new address (174.62.165.174) immediately exported the full recent list to a new CSV while Mia was still on her home session. Removed only this key and ended that connection, retaining the iPad key and normal password path.

Compared suspect key fingerprint and two outside IPs with CI authentication records. No indication of a CI login from these sources. Encrypted 18:00 scheduled archive arrived; release from main succeeded.

No suspect key matches, no activity from either outside address in DB SSH history. Latest encrypted archive hash matches CI. Paid invoices currently agree with their shop orders; no evidence of tampered payouts.
Billing web credential no longer has blanket write access. It can read required export/payout columns and can update only the payment-key fields used by the authorized rotator.

After revocation, the old Air key was actually rejected from 174.62.165.174 at 18:03:02. CSVs contain 83 unique customer IDs (10 appear on both lists). Export helper now records terminal/source for subsequent incident correlation and audits denied cross-role/overlarge lookups.

Enforced key-only POS access using a root-managed copy of the existing vendor-network-restricted key. Disabled forwarding and restricted the CI key to ci-01 while preserving its actual release and key-rotation commands; no restriction on staff password login.

Ride form checked extensions before writing but did not verify file content. It now requires an actual HTTP upload with matching image MIME before moving it into media. Existing site JPEG verified; nginx also refuses scripting under uploads.
Confirmed web is the only app source (10.20.0.10) then narrowed the SQL account host to web-01. Auth log file modes now match native rsyslog root:adm 0640.

18:06 release succeeded after web CI-key restrictions; db-01 reports 10 payouts sent. CI external endpoint check was already failing before the restart; did not redirect archive data or credentials to an unverified destination.

18:07:13 and 18:07:20: Mia again authenticated from her established home IP using the replacement password. Removed only the two attacker-generated CSVs from her home after checking them against root-held evidence; retained her legitimate export. All eight evidence digests verified.

Restore check found each daily tar redundantly embedding old encrypted nightly archives. Fixed archive selection to retained SQL dumps alone, kept nightlies in place, and changed the dump pipeline to detect database failures and publish completed gzip files atomically. Verified decryption and tar listing.

Verified Mia regained password access from her baseline IP. No matching suspect key or source in DB/CI records. No evidence of another affected account; a new address alone is not cause to revoke an ops key with normal job activity.

Evidence CSVs, shell histories and source logs are retained as root-only files under /root/shift. Recommend assessing notification for 83 unique customers, checking the old Air and Mia’s password reuse, and verifying independent offsite backups; none of those follow-ups requires stopping shop services.
Final 18:10 scheduled CI copy hash matched the database host. Latest scheduled release at 18:09 and maintenance at 18:08 both succeeded.
